The story is a highly original piece of writing that avoids cliches in both its language and its plot. Rather than relying on tired expressions, the author crafts fresh, evocative similes and metaphors—such as comparing a postpartum body to "a coat handed back to me by a stranger at a party, still warm from someone else," or holding a baby to "holding a loaf of bread that is also holding you." 

Furthermore, the plot takes a classic trope—babies accidentally being switched at the hospital—and completely subverts the expected, cliched reaction of panic and frantic searching. Instead, the narrator experiences a surreal, dreamlike acceptance and "plain and enormous" happiness, using the mix-up as a poignant metaphor for how all newborns are initially strangers to their mothers.
